papers.abstract: Visual Foundation Models (VFMs) provide semantic cues such as depth and segmentation useful for robotic manipulation, but directly deploying them in closed-loop control is impractical due to high computational cost, temporal inconsistency, and distribution shift between static internet images and egocentric robot observations. We propose All-For-One (AFO), a two-stage distillation framework that leverages VFMs strictly as privileged information during training, using downstream robotic data. Following the privileged learning paradigm, AFO decouples semantic representation learning from inference-time policy execution. In the All stage, a teacher policy fuses RGB observations with outputs from multiple VFMs to learn a semantically enriched representation. In the For-One stage, this knowledge is distilled in-distribution into a lightweight RGB-only student policy. Evaluated on two Adroit tasks and five MetaWorld tasks in simulation, as well as three real-world manipulation tasks, AFO outperforms prior foundation-model-based approaches while using over 30x fewer parameters than VFM-based encoders and 50x lower latency than its own teacher in simulation benchmarks, providing an efficient pathway for transferring foundation-model knowledge to robotic control.
bullets: Addresses the high cost, temporal inconsistency, and observation-distribution mismatch of deploying VFMs directly in closed-loop control.
Uses a two-stage privileged-learning framework: a teacher combines RGB with multiple VFM outputs, then transfers the learned representation to an RGB-only student.
The student performs inference without VFMs, decoupling semantic representation learning from policy execution.
Evaluated on Adroit and MetaWorld simulation tasks plus three real-world manipulation tasks.
Reports over 30× fewer parameters than VFM-based encoders and 50× lower latency than its teacher in simulation, while outperforming prior foundation-model-based approaches.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the All-For-One (AFO) Framework. (a) All. A teacher network employs multiple VFMs (e.g., Molmo [10], SAM 2 [46], and DAM 2 [58]) with learnable lightweight encoders (fT RGB, fT object, f T depth). The resulting representations are aggregated and used to train a policy with a BC loss. (b) For One. A student lightweight RGB encoder (fS RGB) solely learns from the teacher network via a feature distillation loss with BC loss, which benefits from the rich knowledge of large VFMs.

Figure 4. Failure Analysis of VFM-Based Teacher Policies. Directly using VFMs in the teacher introduces brittle failure modes. (a) Segmentation errors: SAM 2 misses the target or masks an irrelevant object. (b) Depth errors: DAM 2 mis-estimates geometry, e.g., predicting a shadow as a closer surface. (c) Temporal inconsistencies: depth estimates fluctuate across adjacent frames. (d) These errors substantially degrade performance: on Adroit Relocate, the teacher succeeds 87% without VFM errors, but only 45% when an error occurs.

Figure 3. Visual illustration of the simulation and real-world benchmarks. We adopt the Adroit [44] and MetaWorld [59] tasks as our simulated environments, and clutter sweep, clean toolbox, and pick-and-place as our real-world tasks. We further evaluate under visual distribution shifts, including desk mat and lighting changes and increased clutter.

Figure 1. Overcoming the Compute–Performance Tradeoff. Learning from scratch (LfS) [17] is fast but inaccurate, whereas VFM backbones [35, 37, 39, 43, 50] are accurate but slow. By distilling large-scale pretrained VFMs [10, 46, 58] into a compact student, AFO attains high success rates while remaining computationally efficient at inference.

Table 1. AFO outperforms all baselines at minimal computational cost. AFO’s student matches or surpasses VFM-based baselines on Adroit and MetaWorld while running at the lowest latency and parameter count, on par with the smallest from-scratch baseline (LfS).

Table 2. Comparison on Real-world Imitation Learning. Success rates under in-distribution (ID) and visual out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions on three real-world tasks. While all methods perform comparably in distribution, AFO degrades far less under visual shifts, surpassing both baselines by a large margin in OOD at the same cost as the lightweight ACT.

Table 5. Comprehensive Ablation Studies. Removing a teacher modality costs more than changing the distillation configuration: dropping segmentation degrades performance noticeably, whereas the loss, alignment, and λ variants all remain close to our default.

Table 3. Effect of teacher modalities on distillation. Depth and segmentation each improve the teacher, but teacher accuracy does not predict distillation quality: only the teacher with both modalities yields the best RGB-only student (2.11 ms, 2.72M).
Table 4. Comprehensive Comparison with Theia Distillation Objective. The first row is the original Theia and the last row is AFO (Student); the two middle rows vary one factor at a time.

papers.selection_reason: Distills visual foundation model knowledge into a fast, lightweight RGB-only visuomotor policy for robotic manipulation, directly fitting learned robot control and manipulation.
papers.title: All-For-One: Distilling Visual Foundation Models to a Fast, Memory-Efficient Visuomotor Policy
papers.tldr: AFO distills privileged visual foundation-model knowledge into a lightweight RGB-only policy for fast, memory-efficient robotic manipulation.

papers.abstract: Large language models provide a variety of responses at inference (generation) that conventionally depend on a temperature parameter. Using a conditional mutual information approach, a quantitative, entropy based analysis of response variety is given. Three limiting behaviors are defined: arbiter, independent (conditionally) and neutral (deterministic) that span no to maximal mutual information. We give examples of each behavior and suggest their application to: temperature analysis, language analysis, prompt compression, and knowledge graphs.
bullets: Defines an entropy-based measure of response variety using conditional mutual information.
Introduces three limiting behaviors: arbiter, conditionally independent, and neutral (deterministic).
These behaviors span a range from no to maximal mutual information.
Provides examples and discusses applications to temperature analysis, language analysis, prompt compression, and knowledge graphs.

figures.caption: Table 1. Arbiter examples. This circumstance should be more likely for longer phrases, such as poetry/lyrics.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a conditional mutual information framework for analyzing LLM response variety, transferable to LLM sampling behavior, prompt compression, and language model analysis.
papers.title: A Conditional Mutual Information Analysis of Response Variety in Language Models
papers.tldr: The paper uses conditional mutual information to quantify and categorize the variety of language-model responses beyond temperature-based analysis.

papers.abstract: Alignment does not eliminate behavioral errors in language models. Models may still refuse benign requests, call unnecessary tools, or yield to false user claims. Current methods mitigate such errors as a computation problem, and rarely explore if the desired behavior is already encoded in the model's representation. Motivated by the observation that behavior-relevant information remains linearly decodable from the final hidden state even when the resulting logits produce the undesired behavior, we introduce HeadEdit, a gradient-free method that calibrates model behavior through the unembedding matrix. HeadEdit extracts a low-rank behavioral subspace from paired completions and uses each prompt's coordinates within it to generate a vocabulary-wide correction, thereby implementing implicitly adaptive steering without manually specified target tokens or parameter updates. HeadEdit improves all nine experimental settings across three tasks and three model families, with negligible inference overhead and no systematic loss of general capabilities. It also reveals a connection to gradient-based alignment. HeadEdit's low-dimensional representation partly predicts how preference tuning changes output logits on unseen prompts. The subspace learned from the model can also be reused after tuning, improving performance without re-extracting or retuning. These results show that HeadEdit provides a practical, lightweight, and interpretable way to calibrate model behavior through the unembedding matrix.
bullets: Addresses residual behavioral errors such as unnecessary refusals, tool calls, and susceptibility to false user claims.
Uses paired completions to learn behavior-relevant directions, then steers outputs without gradients, parameter updates, or manually chosen target tokens.
Improves performance across nine settings spanning three tasks and three model families, with negligible inference overhead and no systematic loss of general capabilities.
The learned subspace partly predicts preference-tuning logit changes on unseen prompts and can be reused after tuning without re-extraction.
Provides a lightweight, interpretable link between representation-based steering and gradient-based alignment.

papers.selection_reason: Gradient-free method for calibrating LLM behavior via the unembedding matrix; relevant to LLM research and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: HeadEdit: Calibrating Language Model Behavior Through the Frozen Unembedding Matrix
papers.tldr: HeadEdit calibrates language-model behavior by extracting a low-rank behavioral subspace and applying adaptive vocabulary-wide corrections through the frozen unembedding matrix.

papers.abstract: We study an endogenous nonstationary stochastic bandit problem with latent linear dynamics, where actions affect both immediate rewards and the future evolution of an unobserved latent state. Rewards are bilinear in the current action and latent state, inducing history-dependent rewards and a nontrivial long-horizon planning problem. The existing explore-then-commit approach achieves $\tilde{O}(T^{2/3})$ regret by uniformly exploring to estimate the latent dynamics and then committing to an optimized open-loop action sequence. We show that this rate can be improved via adaptive block-level optimism. Our key step is a cyclic approximation: under stable dynamics, the infinite-memory reward process can be truncated, and the open-loop benchmark can be approximated by optimizing a finite-memory block-level proxy. Building on this reduction, we propose a UCB-based block algorithm that maintains confidence sets for the truncated dynamics parameters and selects blocks optimistically. We prove a regret bound of order $\tilde{O}(\sqrt T)$, significantly improving over the previous $\tilde{O}(T^{2/3})$ guarantee for the same model. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first $\tilde{O}(\sqrt T)$ regret guarantee for latent linear-dynamics bandits with bilinear reward observations and an open-loop action-sequence benchmark.
bullets: Actions influence both immediate bilinear rewards and an unobserved evolving state, creating history dependence and long-horizon planning challenges.
Stable dynamics enable truncating the infinite-memory reward process and approximating the open-loop benchmark with a finite-memory block proxy.
The proposed UCB-based method maintains confidence sets for truncated dynamics and selects action blocks optimistically.
The analysis establishes a \(\tilde O(\sqrt T)\) regret guarantee for the model and benchmark studied.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Cumulative reward on latent linear-dynamics bandit instances with different stability levels.
Figure 2: Cumulative reward on delayed latent linear-dynamics bandit instances with different levels of stability and delay.

papers.selection_reason: Presents adaptive online learning under nonstationary latent dynamics, fitting online learning and sequential adaptation interests.
papers.title: Block Optimism for Nonstationary Bandits with Latent Linear Dynamics
papers.tldr: A block-level optimism algorithm improves regret for latent linear-dynamics bandits from \(\tilde O(T^{2/3})\) to \(\tilde O(\sqrt T)\).

papers.abstract: Long-term object search requires learning where objects usually appear from repeated but uneven observations of a changing environment. We formulate retrospective open-vocabulary memory as probabilistic inference from censored observations, where the key idea is to reason with evidence per opportunity: a detection or non-detection should influence belief only in proportion to the robot's opportunity to observe the corresponding location. We introduce ECROM, which uses this principle to estimate long-term prevalence for concepts specified only at query time and converts the resulting belief directly into an active-search prior. To evaluate this problem, we introduce a controlled long-term benchmark in ten HM3D homes that independently varies object placement and observation opportunity across repeated traversals. ECROM improves support-level AP on held-out queries by 4.5 points and search SPL by 4.2 points over the strongest competing memory in each metric. The benchmark, dataset, and code will be open-sourced. Project page: https://jiaming.im/ecrom/
bullets: Addresses learning object-location prevalence from repeated, uneven observations.
Models detections and non-detections as censored evidence weighted by observation opportunity.
Supports concepts specified only at query time and converts beliefs into active-search priors.
Evaluated on a controlled benchmark spanning ten HM3D homes with varied placements and observation opportunities.
Improves support-level AP by 4.5 points and search SPL by 4.2 points over the strongest competing memory in each metric.

figures.caption: Figure 2: System overview. (1) During query-independent mapping, RGB-D traversals are organized into a place–view atlas with surface supports and per-episode observation opportunities cje. (2) At query time, open-vocabulary detector responses are lifted to supports and combined with opportunity to infer the long-term prevalence posterior p(θj | Hj , q) (Section 4.3). (3) The resulting belief guides budgeted active search and is updated after each executed view (Eq. 8).

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses long-term robot object search with memory-driven active-search priors, fitting embodied navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: Retrospective Open-Vocabulary Memory for Long-Term Object Search
papers.tldr: ECROM uses opportunity-aware probabilistic memory to improve long-term open-vocabulary object search in changing environments.
